{{Short description|Topological vector spaces}}
{{about|the topological vector spaces used to define and use Schwartz distributions|more basic information about distributions and operations on them|Distribution (mathematics)}}
{{technical|reason=The lead, in particular, the first paragraph are unnecessary technical.|date=July 2024}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''spaces of test functions and distributions''' are [[topological vector space]]s (TVSs) that are used in the definition and application of [[Distribution (mathematics)|distributions]]. 
Test functions are usually [[Smooth function|infinitely differentiable]] [[Complex number|complex]]-valued (or sometimes [[Real number|real]]-valued) functions on a non-empty [[Open set|open subset]] <math>U \subseteq \R^n</math> that have [[Compact space|compact]] [[Support (mathematics)|support]]. 
The space of all test functions, denoted by {{tmath| C^\infty_\text{c}(U) }}, is endowed with a certain topology, called the {{em|canonical [[LF-space|LF-topology]]}}, that makes <math>C^\infty_\text{c}(U)</math> into a [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[topological vector space|TVS]]. 
The [[strong dual space]] of <math>C^\infty_\text{c}(U)</math> is called {{em|'''the''' space of distributions on <math>U</math>}} and is denoted by <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) := \left(C^\infty_\text{c}(U)\right)^{\prime}_b,</math> where the "<math>b</math>" subscript indicates that the [[continuous dual space]] of <math>C^\infty_\text{c}(U),</math> denoted by <math>\left(C^\infty_\text{c}(U)\right)^{\prime},</math> is endowed with the [[strong dual topology]].

There are other possible choices for the space of test functions, which lead to other different [[Vector space|space]]s of distributions. If <math>U = \R^n</math> then the use of [[Schwartz space|Schwartz functions]]<ref group=note>The [[Schwartz space]] consists of smooth rapidly decreasing test functions, where "rapidly decreasing" means that the function decreases faster than any polynomial increases as points in its domain move away from the origin.</ref> as test functions gives rise to a certain subspace of <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> whose elements are called '''{{em|tempered distributions}}'''. These are important because they allow the [[Fourier transform]] to be extended from "standard functions" to tempered distributions. The set of tempered distributions forms a [[Vector space|vector subspace]] of the space of distributions <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> and is thus one example of a space of distributions; there are many other spaces of distributions.

There also exist other major classes of test functions that are {{em|not}} subsets of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, such as spaces of [[Analytic function|analytic test functions]], which produce very different classes of distributions. The theory of such distributions has a different character from the previous one because there are no analytic functions with non-empty compact support.<ref group=note>Except for the trivial (i.e. identically <math>0</math>) map, which of course is always analytic.</ref> Use of analytic test functions leads to [[Mikio Sato|Sato]]'s theory of [[hyperfunction]]s.

== Notation ==

The following notation will be used throughout this article:
* <math>n</math> is a fixed positive [[integer]] and <math>U</math> is a fixed non-empty [[Open set|open subset]] of [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^{n}.</math>
* <math>\N = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}</math> denotes the [[natural number]]s.
* <math>k</math> will denote a non-negative integer or <math>\infty.</math>
* If <math>f</math> is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] then <math>\operatorname{Dom}(f)</math> will denote its [[Domain of a function|domain]] and the '''{{em|[[Support (mathematics)|{{visible anchor|support of a function|text=support}}]]}}''' of <math>f,</math> denoted by <math>\operatorname{supp}(f),</math> is defined to be the [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of the set <math>\{x \in \operatorname{Dom}(f): f(x) \neq 0\}</math> in <math>\operatorname{Dom}(f).</math>
* For two functions <math>f, g : U \to \Complex</math>, the following notation defines a canonical [[Dual system|pairing]]: <math display=block>\langle f, g\rangle := \int_U f(x) g(x) \,dx.</math>
* A '''{{em|[[Multi-index notation|multi-index]]}} of size''' <math>n</math> is an element in <math>\N^n</math> (given that <math>n</math> is fixed, if the size of multi-indices is omitted then the size should be assumed to be <math>n</math>). The '''{{em|length}}''' of a multi-index <math>\alpha = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n) \in \N^n</math> is defined as <math>\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n</math> and denoted by <math>|\alpha|.</math> Multi-indices are particularly useful when dealing with functions of several variables, in particular we introduce the following notations for a given multi-index <math>\alpha = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n) \in \N^n</math>: <math display=block>\begin{align}
x^\alpha &= x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_n^{\alpha_n} \\
\partial^\alpha &= \frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}}{\partial x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots \partial x_n^{\alpha_n}}
\end{align}</math> We also introduce a partial order of all multi-indices by <math>\beta \geq \alpha</math> if and only if <math>\beta_i \geq \alpha_i</math> for all <math>1 \leq i\leq n.</math> When <math>\beta \geq \alpha</math> we define their multi-index binomial coefficient as: <math display=block>\binom{\beta}{\alpha} := \binom{\beta_1}{\alpha_1} \cdots \binom{\beta_n}{\alpha_n}.</math>
* <math>\mathbb{K}</math> will denote a certain non-empty collection of compact subsets of <math>U</math> (described in detail below).

== Definitions of test functions and distributions ==

In this section, we will formally define real-valued distributions on {{mvar|U}}. With minor modifications, one can also define complex-valued distributions, and one can replace <math>\R^n</math> with any ([[Paracompactness|paracompact]]) [[smooth manifold]].

{{block indent|em=1.5|text='''Notation''': 
# Let <math>k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty\}.</math>
# Let <math>C^k(U)</math> denote the [[vector space]] of all {{mvar|k}}-times [[continuously differentiable]] real or complex-valued functions on {{mvar|U}}.
# For any compact subset <math>K \subseteq U,</math> let <math>C^k(K)</math> and <math>C^k(K;U)</math> both denote the vector space of all those functions <math>f \in C^k(U)</math> such that {{tmath| \operatorname{supp}(f) \subseteq K }}. 
#* If <math>f \in C^k(K)</math> then the domain of <math>f</math> is {{mvar|U}} and not {{mvar|K}}. So although <math>C^k(K)</math> depends on both {{mvar|K}} and {{mvar|U}}, only {{mvar|K}} is typically indicated. The justification for this common practice is [[#Omitting the open set from notation|detailed below]]. The notation <math>C^k(K;U)</math> will only be used when the notation <math>C^k(K)</math> risks being ambiguous.
#* Every <math>C^k(K)</math> contains the constant {{math|0}} map, even if <math>K = \varnothing.</math>
# Let <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> denote the set of all <math>f \in C^k(U)</math> such that <math>f \in C^k(K)</math> for some compact subset {{mvar|K}} of {{mvar|U}}.
#* Equivalently, <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is the set of all <math>f \in C^k(U)</math> such that <math>f</math> has compact [[#support of a function|support]].
#* <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is equal to the union of all <math>C^k(K)</math> as <math>K</math> ranges over {{tmath| \mathbb{K} }}.
#* If <math>f</math> is a real-valued function on {{mvar|U}}, then <math>f</math> is an element of <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> if and only if <math>f</math> is a <math>C^k</math> [[bump function]]. Every real-valued test function on <math>U</math> is always also a complex-valued test function on <math>U.</math>
}}

[[File:Bump.png|thumb|350x350px|The graph of the [[bump function]] <math>(x,y) \in \mathbf{R}^2 \mapsto \Psi(r),</math> where <math>r = (x^2 + y^2)^\frac{1}{2}</math> and <math>\Psi(r) = e^{-\frac{1}{1 - r^2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\{|r|<1\}}.</math> This function is a test function on <math>\R^2</math> and is an element of <math>C^\infty_\text{c}\left(\R^2\right).</math> The [[#support of a function|support]] of this function is the closed [[unit disk]] in <math>\R^2.</math> It is non-zero on the open unit disk and it is equal to {{math|0}} everywhere outside of it.]]

Note that for all <math>j, k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty\}</math> and any compact subsets {{mvar|K}} and {{mvar|L}} of {{mvar|U}}, we have:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
C^k(K) &\subseteq C^k_\text{c}(U) \subseteq C^k(U) \\
C^k(K) &\subseteq C^k(L) && \text{ if } K \subseteq L \\
C^k(K) &\subseteq C^j(K) && \text{ if } j \leq k \\
C_\text{c}^k(U) &\subseteq C^j_\text{c}(U) && \text{ if } j \leq k \\
C^k(U) &\subseteq C^j(U) && \text{ if } j \leq k \\
\end{align}</math>

{{block indent|em=1.5|text='''Definition''': Elements of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> are called '''{{em|test functions}}''' on {{mvar|U}} and <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is called the '''{{em|space of test functions}}''' on {{mvar|U}}. We will use both <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> and <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> to denote this space.}}

Distributions on {{mvar|U}} are defined to be the [[continuous linear functional]]s on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> when this vector space is endowed with a particular topology called the '''{{em|canonical LF-topology}}'''.  
This topology is unfortunately not easy to define but it is nevertheless still possible to characterize distributions in a way so that no mention of the canonical LF-topology is made.

'''Proposition''': If {{mvar|T}} is a [[Linear form|linear functional]] on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> then the {{mvar|T}} is a distribution if and only if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:
# For every compact subset <math>K\subseteq U</math> there exist constants <math>C>0</math> and <math>N\in \N</math> (dependent on <math>K</math>) such that for all <math>f \in C^\infty(K),</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=222-223}} <math display=block>|T(f)| \leq C \sup \{|\partial^\alpha f(x)|: x \in U, |\alpha| \leq N\}.</math>
# For every compact subset <math>K\subseteq U</math> there exist constants <math>C>0</math> and <math>N\in \N</math> such that for all <math>f \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> with [[#support of a function|support]] contained in <math>K,</math><ref name="Grubb 2009 page=14">See for example {{harvnb|Grubb|2009|page=14}}.</ref> <math display=block>|T(f)| \leq C \sup \{|\partial^\alpha f(x)| : x \in K, |\alpha|\leq N\}.</math>
# For any compact subset <math>K\subseteq U</math> and any sequence <math>\{f_i\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C^\infty(K),</math> if <math>\{\partial^\alpha f_i\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> converges uniformly to zero on <math>K</math> for all [[Multi-index|multi-indices]] <math>\alpha</math>, then <math>T(f_i) \to 0.</math>

The above characterizations can be used to determine whether or not a linear functional is a distribution, but more advanced uses of distributions and test functions (such as applications to [[differential equations]]) is limited if no topologies are placed on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> and {{tmath| \mathcal{D}(U) }}.  
To define the space of distributions we must first define the canonical LF-topology, which in turn requires that several other [[locally convex]] [[topological vector space]]s (TVSs) be defined first. First, a ([[Normable space|non-normable]]) topology on <math>C^\infty(U)</math> will be defined, then every <math>C^\infty(K)</math> will be endowed with the [[subspace topology]] induced on it by {{tmath| C^\infty(U) }}, and finally the ([[Metrizable space|non-metrizable]]) canonical LF-topology on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> will be defined.
The space of distributions, being defined as the [[continuous dual space]] of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, is then endowed with the (non-metrizable) [[Strong topology (polar topology)|strong dual topology]] induced by <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> and the canonical LF-topology (this topology is a generalization of the usual [[operator norm]] induced topology that is placed on the continuous dual spaces of [[normed space]]s). 
This finally permits consideration of more advanced notions such as convergence of distributions (both sequences {{em|and}} nets), various (sub)spaces of distributions, and operations on distributions, including extending differential equations to distributions.

=== Choice of compact sets K ===

Throughout, <math>\mathbb{K}</math> will be any collection of compact subsets of <math>U</math> such that (1) <math display=inline>U = \bigcup_{K \in \mathbb{K}} K,</math> and (2) for any compact <math>K_1,K_2 \subseteq U</math> there exists some <math>K \in \mathbb{K}</math> such that <math>K_1\cup K_2 \subseteq K.</math> The most common choices for <math>\mathbb{K}</math> are:
* The set of all compact subsets of {{tmath| U }}, or
* A set <math>\left\{\overline{U}_1, \overline{U}_2, \ldots \right\}</math> where <math display="inline">U = \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i,</math> and for all {{mvar|i}}, <math>\overline{U}_i \subseteq U_{i+1}</math> and <math>U_i</math> is a [[relatively compact]] non-empty open subset of <math>U</math> (here, "relatively compact" means that the [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of {{tmath| U_i }}, in either {{mvar|U}} or {{tmath| \R^n }}, is compact).

We make <math>\mathbb{K}</math> into a [[directed set]] by defining <math>K_1 \leq K_2</math> if and only if <math>K_1 \subseteq K_2.</math> Note that although the definitions of the subsequently defined topologies explicitly reference {{tmath| \mathbb{K} }}, in reality they do not depend on the choice of <math>\mathbb{K};</math> that is, if <math>\mathbb{K}_1</math> and <math>\mathbb{K}_2</math> are any two such collections of compact subsets of <math>U,</math> then the topologies defined on <math>C^k(U)</math> and <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> by using <math>\mathbb{K}_1</math> in place of <math>\mathbb{K}</math> are the same as those defined by using <math>\mathbb{K}_2</math> in place of <math>\mathbb{K}.</math>

=== Topology on ''C''<sup>''k''</sup>(''U'') ===

We now introduce the [[seminorm]]s that will define the topology on <math>C^k(U).</math> Different authors sometimes use different families of seminorms so we list the most common families below. However, the resulting topology is the same no matter which family is used.
<!---- START: Removed ----
This is one reason why, of all the possible spaces of maps that we could consider, we chose to consider the spaces <math>C^k(U)</math> of {{mvar|k}}-times [[continuously differentiable]] maps. 
------ END: Removed ---->

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=Suppose <math>k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty\}</math> and <math>K</math> is an arbitrary compact subset of <math>U.</math> Suppose <math>i</math> an integer such that <math>0 \leq i \leq k</math><ref group=note>Note that <math>i</math> being an integer implies <math>i \neq \infty.</math> This is sometimes expressed as <math>0 \leq i < k + 1.</math> Since <math>\infty + 1 = \infty,</math> the inequality "<math>0 \leq i < k + 1</math>" means: <math>0 \leq i < \infty</math> if <math>k = \infty,</math> while if <math>k \neq \infty</math> then it means <math>0 \leq i \leq k.</math></ref> and <math>p</math> is a multi-index with length <math>| p|\leq k.</math> For <math>K \neq \varnothing,</math> define:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\text{ (1) }\ & s_{p,K}(f) &&:= \sup_{x_0 \in K} \left| \partial^p f(x_0) \right| \\[4pt]
\text{ (2) }\ & r_{i,K}(f) &&:= \sup_{\stackrel{|p| \leq i}{x_0 \in K}}  \left| \partial^p f(x_0) \right| = \sup_{|p| \leq i} \left(s_{p, K}(f)\right) \\[4pt]
\text{ (3) }\ & t_{i,K}(f) &&:= \sup_{x_0 \in K} \left(\sum_{|p| \leq i} \left| \partial^p f(x_0) \right|\right)
\end{alignat}</math>
while for <math>K = \varnothing,</math> define all the functions above to be the constant {{math|0}} map. 
}}
All of the functions above are non-negative <math>\R</math>-valued<ref group="note">The image of the compact set <math>K</math> under a continuous <math>\R</math>-valued map (for example, <math>x \mapsto \left|\partial^p f(x)\right|</math> for <math>x \in U</math>) is itself a [[Compact set|compact]], and thus bounded, subset of <math>\R.</math> If <math>K \neq \varnothing</math> then this implies that each of the functions defined above is <math>\R</math>-valued (that is, none of the [[Infimum and supremum|supremums]] above are ever equal to {{tmath| \infty }}).</ref> [[seminorm]]s on <math>C^k(U).</math> As explained in [[Locally convex topological vector space#Definition via seminorms|this article]], every set of seminorms on a vector space induces a [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[Topological vector space|vector topology]].

Each of the following sets of seminorms 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
A ~:= \quad &\{r_{i,K} &&: \;K \text{ compact and } \;&&i \in \N \text{ satisfies } \;&&0 \leq i \leq k\} \\
B ~:= \quad &\{t_{i,K} &&: \;K \text{ compact and } \;&&i \in \N \text{ satisfies } \;&&0 \leq i \leq k\} \\
C ~:= \quad &\{s_{p,K} &&: \;K \text{ compact and } \;&&p \in \N^n \text{ satisfies } \;&&|p| \leq k\}
\end{alignat}</math>
generate the same [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[Topological vector space|vector topology]] on <math>C^k(U)</math>.

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=The vector space <math>C^k(U)</math> is endowed with the [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] topology induced by any one of the four families <math>A, B, C</math> of seminorms described above.}}

With this topology, <math>C^k(U)</math> becomes a locally convex [[Fréchet space]] that is {{em|not}} [[Normable space|normable]]. Every element of <math>A \cup B \cup C</math> is a continuous seminorm on {{tmath| C^k(U) }}.
Under this topology, a [[net (mathematics)|net]] <math>(f_i)_{i\in I}</math> in <math>C^k(U)</math> converges to <math>f \in C^k(U)</math> if and only if for every multi-index <math>p</math> with <math>|p|< k + 1</math> and every compact {{tmath| K }}, the net of partial derivatives <math>\left(\partial^p f_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> [[Uniform convergence|converges uniformly]] to <math>\partial^p f</math> on <math>K.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=85-89}} For any <math>k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty\},</math> any [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|(von Neumann) bounded subset]] of <math>C^{k+1}(U)</math> is a [[relatively compact]] subset of <math>C^k(U).</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=142-149}} In particular, a subset of <math>C^\infty(U)</math> is bounded if and only if it is bounded in <math>C^i(U)</math> for all <math>i \in \N.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=142-149}} The space <math>C^k(U)</math> is a [[Montel space]] if and only if <math>k = \infty.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=356-358}}

The topology on <math>C^\infty(U)</math> is the superior limit of the [[Subspace topology|subspace topologies]] induced on <math>C^\infty(U)</math> by the TVSs <math>C^i(U)</math> as {{mvar|i}} ranges over the non-negative integers.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=85-89}} A subset <math>W</math> of <math>C^\infty(U)</math> is open in this topology if and only if there exists <math>i\in \N</math> such that <math>W</math> is open when <math>C^\infty(U)</math> is endowed with the [[subspace topology]] induced on it by {{tmath| C^i(U) }}.

==== Metric defining the topology ====

If the family of compact sets <math>\mathbb{K} = \left\{\overline{U}_1, \overline{U}_2, \ldots \right\}</math> satisfies <math display=inline>U = \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty U_j</math> and <math>\overline{U}_i \subseteq U_{i+1}</math> for all <math>i,</math> then a complete translation-invariant [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] on <math>C^\infty(U)</math> can be obtained by taking a suitable countable [[Fréchet combination]] of any one of the above defining families of seminorms (''A'', ''B'', ''C''). For example, using the seminorms <math>(r_{i,K_i})_{i=1}^\infty</math> results in the metric <math display=block>d(f, g) := \sum^\infty_{i=1} \frac{1}{2^i} \frac{r_{i, \overline{U}_i}(f - g)}{1 + r_{i, \overline{U}_i}(f - g)} = \sum^\infty_{i=1} \frac{1}{2^i} \frac{\sup_{|p| \leq i, x \in \overline{U}_i}  \left| \partial^p (f - g)(x) \right|}{\left[ 1 + \sup_{|p| \leq i, x \in \overline{U}_i}  \left| \partial^p (f - g)(x) \right| \right]}.</math>

Often, it is easier to just consider seminorms (avoiding any metric) and use the tools of [[functional analysis]].

=== Topology on ''C''<sup>''k''</sup>(''K'') ===

As before, fix <math>k \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty\}.</math> Recall that if <math>K</math> is any compact subset of <math>U</math> then <math>C^k(K) \subseteq C^k(U).</math>

{{block indent|em=1.5|text='''Assumption''': For any compact subset <math>K \subseteq U,</math> we will henceforth assume that <math>C^k(K)</math> is endowed with the [[subspace topology]] it inherits from the [[Fréchet space]] <math>C^k(U).</math>}}

For any compact subset <math>K \subseteq U,</math> <math>C^k(K)</math> is a closed subspace of the Fréchet space <math>C^k(U)</math> and is thus also a [[Fréchet space]]. For all compact <math>K, L \subseteq U</math> satisfying <math>K \subseteq L,</math> denote the [[inclusion map]] by <math>\operatorname{In}_K^L : C^k(K) \to C^k(L).</math> Then this map is a linear embedding of TVSs (that is, it is a [[linear map]] that is also a [[topological embedding]]) whose [[Image (mathematics)|image]] (or "range") is closed in its [[codomain]]; said differently, the topology on <math>C^k(K)</math> is identical to the subspace topology it inherits from <math>C^k(L),</math> and also <math>C^k(K)</math> is a closed subset of <math>C^k(L).</math> The [[Topological interior|interior]] of <math>C^\infty(K)</math> relative to <math>C^\infty(U)</math> is empty.{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=149-181}}

If <math>k</math> is finite then <math>C^k(K)</math> is a [[Banach space]]{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-134}} with a topology that can be defined by the [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]]
<math display=block>r_K(f) := \sup_{|p|<k} \left(\sup_{x_0 \in K} \left| \partial^p f(x_0) \right|\right).</math>

And when <math>k = 2,</math> then <math>\,C^k(K)</math> is even a [[Hilbert space]].{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-134}} The space <math>C^\infty(K)</math> is a [[Distinguished space|distinguished]] [[Schwartz topological vector space|Schwartz]] [[Montel space]] so if <math>C^\infty(K) \neq \{0\}</math> then it is {{em|not}} [[Normable space|normable]] and thus {{em|not}} a Banach space (although like all other <math>C^k(K),</math> it is a [[Fréchet space]]).

==== Trivial extensions and independence of ''C''<sup>''k''</sup>(''K'')'s topology from ''U'' ====
{{anchor|Omitting the open set from notation}}

The definition of <math>C^k(K)</math> depends on {{mvar|U}} so we will let <math>C^k(K;U)</math> denote the topological space <math>C^k(K),</math> which by definition is a [[topological subspace]] of <math>C^k(U).</math> Suppose <math>V</math> is an open subset of <math>\R^n</math> containing <math>U</math> and for any compact subset {{tmath| K \subseteq V }}, let <math>C^k(K; V)</math> is the vector subspace of <math>C^k(V)</math> consisting of maps with [[#support of a function|support]] contained in <math>K.</math>  Given {{tmath| f \in C_\text{c}^k(U) }}, its {{em|'''trivial extension''' to {{mvar|V}}}} is by definition, the function <math>I(f) := F : V \to \Complex</math> defined by:
<math display=block>F(x) = \begin{cases} f(x) & x \in U, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}</math>
so that <math>F \in C^k(V).</math> Let <math>I : C_\text{c}^k(U) \to C^k(V)</math> denote the map that sends a function in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> to its trivial extension on {{mvar|V}}. This map is a linear [[Injective function|injection]] and for every compact subset <math>K \subseteq U</math> (where <math>K</math> is also a compact subset of <math>V</math> since {{tmath| K \subseteq U \subseteq V }}) we have 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
I\left(C^k(K; U)\right) &~=~ C^k(K; V) \qquad \text{ and thus } \\
I\left(C_\text{c}^k(U)\right) &~\subseteq~ C_\text{c}^k(V)
\end{alignat}</math>
If {{mvar|I}} is restricted to <math>C^k(K; U)</math> then the following induced linear map is a [[homeomorphism]] (and thus a [[TVS-isomorphism]]):
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
 \,& C^k(K; U) && \to \,&& C^k(K;V) \\
   & f                  && \mapsto\,&& I(f) \\
\end{alignat}</math>
and thus the next two maps (which like the previous map are defined by <math>f \mapsto I(f)</math>) are [[topological embedding]]s:
<math display=block>C^k(K; U) \to C^k(V), \qquad \text{ and } \qquad C^k(K; U) \to C_\text{c}^k(V),</math>
(the topology on <math>C_\text{c}^k(V)</math> is the canonical LF topology, which is defined later). 
Using the injection
<math display=block>I : C_\text{c}^k(U) \to C^k(V)</math>
the vector space <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is canonically identified with its image in <math>C_\text{c}^k(V) \subseteq C^k(V)</math> (however, if <math>U \neq V</math> then <math>I : C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to C_\text{c}^\infty(V)</math> is {{em|not}} a [[topological embedding]] when these spaces are endowed with their canonical LF topologies, although it is continuous).{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}}
Because {{tmath| C^k(K; U) \subseteq C_\text{c}^k(U) }}, through this identification, <math>C^k(K; U)</math> can also be considered as a subset of <math>C^k(V).</math> Importantly, the subspace topology <math>C^k(K; U)</math> inherits from <math>C^k(U)</math> (when it is viewed as a subset of <math>C^k(U)</math>) is identical to the subspace topology that it inherits from <math>C^k(V)</math> (when <math>C^k(K; U)</math> is viewed instead as a subset of <math>C^k(V)</math> via the identification). Thus the topology on <math>C^k(K;U)</math> is independent of the open subset {{mvar|U}} of <math>\R^n</math> that contains {{mvar|K}}.{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=149-181}} This justifies the practice of writing <math>C^k(K)</math> instead of {{tmath| C^k(K; U) }}.

=== Canonical LF topology ===

{{see also|LF-space|Topology of uniform convergence}}
Recall that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> denote all those functions in <math>C^k(U)</math> that have compact [[#support of a function|support]] in <math>U,</math> where note that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is the union of all <math>C^k(K)</math> as {{mvar|K}} ranges over <math>\mathbb{K}.</math> Moreover, for every {{mvar|k}}, <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is a dense subset of <math>C^k(U).</math> The special case when <math>k = \infty</math> gives us the space of test functions.

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=<math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is called the {{em|'''space of test functions''' on <math>U</math>}} and it may also be denoted by <math>\mathcal{D}(U).</math>}}

This section defines the canonical LF topology as a [[direct limit]]. It is also possible to define this topology in terms of its neighborhoods of the origin, which is described afterwards.

==== Topology defined by direct limits ====

For any two sets {{mvar|K}} and {{mvar|L}}, we declare that <math>K \leq L</math> if and only if {{tmath| K \subseteq L }}, which in particular makes the collection <math>\mathbb{K}</math> of compact subsets of {{mvar|U}} into a [[directed set]] (we say that such a collection is {{em|'''directed by subset inclusion'''}}). For all compact <math>K, L \subseteq U</math> satisfying <math>K \subseteq L,</math> there are [[inclusion map]]s
<math display=block>\operatorname{In}_K^L : C^k(K) \to C^k(L)\quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{In}_K^U : C^k(K) \to C_\text{c}^k(U).</math>

Recall from above that the map <math>\operatorname{In}_K^L : C^k(K) \to C^k(L)</math> is a [[topological embedding]]. The collection of maps <math display=block>\left\{\operatorname{In}_K^L \;:\; K, L \in \mathbb{K} \;\text{ and }\; K \subseteq L \right\}</math>
forms a [[direct limit|direct system]] in the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of [[locally convex topological vector space]]s that is [[directed set|directed]] by <math>\mathbb{K}</math> (under subset inclusion). This system's [[direct limit]] (in the category of locally convex TVSs) is the pair <math>(C_\text{c}^k(U), \operatorname{In}_{\bullet}^U)</math> where <math>\operatorname{In}_{\bullet}^U := \left(\operatorname{In}_K^U\right)_{K \in \mathbb{K}}</math> are the natural inclusions and where <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is now endowed with the (unique) [[Comparison of topologies|strongest]] locally convex topology making all of the inclusion maps <math>\operatorname{In}_\bullet^U = (\operatorname{In}_K^U)_{K \in \mathbb{K}}</math> continuous.

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=The {{em|'''canonical LF topology''' on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math>}} is the [[Final topology|finest]] [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] topology on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> making all of the inclusion maps <math>\operatorname{In}_K^U : C^k(K) \to C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> continuous (where {{mvar|K}} ranges over {{tmath| \mathbb{K} }}).}}

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=As is common in mathematics literature, the space <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is henceforth assumed to be endowed with its canonical LF topology (unless explicitly stated otherwise).}}

==== Topology defined by neighborhoods of the origin ====

If <math>\cal U</math> is a [[Convex set|convex]] subset of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}, then <math>\cal U</math> is a [[Neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]] of the origin in the canonical LF topology if and only if it satisfies the following condition:

{{NumBlk|:|For all {{tmath| K \in \mathbb{K} }}, <math>{\cal U}\cap C^k(K)</math> is a neighborhood of the origin in {{tmath| C^k(K) }}.|{{EquationRef|CN}}}}

Note that any convex set satisfying this condition is necessarily [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] in {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}. Since the topology of any [[topological vector space]] is translation-invariant, any TVS-topology is completely determined by the set of neighborhood of the origin. This means that one could actually {{em|define}} the canonical LF topology by declaring that a convex [[Balanced set|balanced]] subset {{mvar|U}} is a neighborhood of the origin if and only if it satisfies condition {{EquationNote|CN}}.

==== Topology defined via differential operators ====

A {{em|'''linear [[differential operator]] in {{mvar|U}} with smooth coefficients'''}} is a sum
<math display=block>P := \sum_{\alpha \in \N^n} c_\alpha \partial^\alpha</math>
where <math>c_\alpha \in C^\infty(U)</math> and all but finitely many of <math>c_\alpha</math> are identically {{math|0}}. The integer <math>\sup \{|\alpha|: c_\alpha \neq 0\}</math> is called the {{em|'''order'''}} of the differential operator <math>P.</math> If <math>P</math> is a linear differential operator of order {{mvar|k}} then it induces a canonical linear map <math>C^k(U) \to C^0(U)</math> defined by <math>\phi \mapsto P\phi,</math> where we shall reuse notation and also denote this map by <math>P.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=247-252}}

For any <math>1 \leq k \leq \infty,</math> the canonical LF topology on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is the weakest locally convex TVS topology making all linear differential operators in <math>U</math> of order <math>\,< k + 1</math> into continuous maps from <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> into {{tmath| C_\text{c}^0(U) }}.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=247-252}}

==== Properties of the canonical LF topology ====
===== Canonical LF topology's independence from {{math|K}} =====

One benefit of defining the canonical LF topology as the direct limit of a [[direct limit|direct system]] is that we may immediately use the universal property of direct limits. Another benefit is that we can use well-known results from [[category theory]] to deduce that the canonical LF topology is actually independent of the particular choice of the [[directed set|directed]] collection <math>\mathbb{K}</math> of compact sets. And by considering different collections <math>\mathbb{K}</math> (in particular, those <math>\mathbb{K}</math> mentioned at the beginning of this article), we may deduce different properties of this topology. In particular, we may deduce that the canonical LF topology makes <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> into a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[locally convex]] [[LF-space|strict LF-space]] (and also a [[LB-space|strict LB-space]] if <math>k \neq \infty</math>), which of course is the reason why this topology is called "the canonical LF topology" (see this footnote for more details).<ref group=note>If we take <math>\mathbb{K}</math> to be the set of {{em|all}} compact subsets of {{mvar|U}} then we can use the universal property of direct limits to conclude that the inclusion <math>\operatorname{In}_K^U : C^k(K) \to C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is a continuous and even that they are topological embedding for every compact subset <math>K \subseteq U.</math> If however, we take <math>\mathbb{K}</math> to be the set of closures of some countable increasing sequence of relatively compact open subsets of {{mvar|U}} having all of the properties mentioned earlier in this in this article then we immediately deduce that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is a Hausdorff locally convex [[LF-space|strict LF-space]] (and even a [[LB-space|strict LB-space]] when <math>k \neq \infty</math>). All of these facts can also be proved directly without using direct systems (although with more work).</ref>

===== Universal property =====

From the universal property of [[direct limit]]s, we know that if <math>u : C_\text{c}^k(U) \to Y</math> is a linear map into a locally convex space {{mvar|Y}} (not necessarily Hausdorff), then {{mvar|u}} is continuous if and only if {{mvar|u}} is [[Bounded linear map|bounded]] if and only if for every {{tmath| K \in \mathbb{K} }}, the restriction of {{mvar|u}} to <math>C^k(K)</math> is continuous (or bounded).{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=126-134}}{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=136-148}}

===== Dependence of the canonical LF topology on {{mvar|U}} =====

Suppose {{mvar|V}} is an open subset of <math>\R^n</math> containing <math>U.</math> Let <math>I : C_\text{c}^k(U)\to C_\text{c}^k(V)</math> denote the map that sends a function in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> to its trivial extension on {{mvar|V}} (which was defined above). This map is a continuous linear map.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}} If (and only if) <math>U \neq V</math> then <math>I\left(C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\right)</math> is {{em|not}} a dense subset of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(V)</math> and <math>I : C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to C_\text{c}^\infty(V)</math> is {{em|not}} a [[topological embedding]].{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}} Consequently, if <math>U \neq V</math> then the transpose of <math>I : C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to C_\text{c}^\infty(V)</math> is neither one-to-one nor onto.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}}

===== Bounded subsets =====

A subset <math>B \subseteq C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded]] in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> if and only if there exists some <math>K \in \mathbb{K}</math> such that <math>B \subseteq C^k(K)</math> and <math>B</math> is a bounded subset of <math>C^k(K).</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=136-148}} Moreover, if <math>K \subseteq U</math> is compact and <math>S \subseteq C^k(K)</math> then <math>S</math> is bounded in <math>C^k(K)</math> if and only if it is bounded in <math>C^k(U).</math> For any <math>0 \leq k \leq \infty,</math> any bounded subset of <math>C_\text{c}^{k+1}(U)</math> (resp. <math>C^{k+1}(U)</math>) is a [[relatively compact]] subset of <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> (resp. {{tmath| C^k(U) }}), where {{tmath|1= \infty + 1 = \infty }}.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=136-148}}

===== Non-metrizability =====

For all compact {{tmath| K \subseteq U }}, the interior of <math>C^k(K)</math> in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is empty so that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is of the first category in itself. It follows from [[Baire category theorem|Baire's theorem]] that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is {{em|not}} [[Metrizable topological vector space|metrizable]] and thus also {{em|not}} [[Normable space|normable]] (see this footnote<ref group=note>For any [[Topological vector space|TVS]] {{mvar|X}} ([[Metrizable space|metrizable]] or otherwise), the notion of [[Complete topological vector space|completeness]] depends entirely on a certain so-called "canonical [[Uniform space|uniformity]]" that is defined using {{em|only}} the subtraction operation (see the article [[Complete topological vector space]] for more details). In this way, the notion of a [[Complete topological vector space|complete TVS]] does not {{em|require}} the existence of any [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]]. However, if the TVS {{mvar|X}} is metrizable and if <math>d</math> is {{em|any}} translation-invariant metric on {{mvar|X}} that defines its topology, then {{mvar|X}} is complete as a TVS (i.e. it is a [[complete uniform space]] under its canonical uniformity) if and only if <math>(X, d)</math> is a [[complete metric space]]. So if a TVS {{mvar|X}} happens to have a topology that can be defined by such a metric {{mvar|d}} then {{mvar|d}} may be used to deduce the completeness of {{mvar|X}} but the existence of such a metric is not necessary for defining completeness and it is even possible to deduce that a metrizable TVS is complete without ever even considering a metric (e.g. since the [[Cartesian product]] of any collection of complete TVSs is again a complete TVS, we can immediately deduce that the TVS <math>\R^\N,</math> which happens to be metrizable, is a complete TVS; note that there was no need to consider any metric on {{tmath| \R^\N }}).</ref> for an explanation of how the non-metrizable space <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> can be complete even though it does not admit a metric). The fact that <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is a [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space]] makes up for the non-metrizability of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> (see this footnote for a more detailed explanation).<ref group=note>One reason for giving <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> the canonical LF topology is because it is with this topology that <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> and its continuous dual space both become nuclear spaces, which have many nice properties and which may be viewed as a generalization of finite-dimensional spaces (for comparison, normed spaces are another generalization of finite-dimensional spaces that have many "nice" properties). In more detail, there are two classes of [[topological vector space]]s (TVSs) that are particularly similar to finite-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]s: the [[Banach space]]s (especially [[Hilbert space]]s) and the [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space]]s. Montel spaces are a class of TVSs in which every closed and bounded subset is compact (this generalizes the [[Heine–Borel theorem]]), which is a property that no infinite-dimensional Banach space can have; that is, no infinite-dimensional TVS can be both a Banach space and a Montel space. Also, no infinite-dimensional TVS can be both a Banach space and a nuclear space. All finite dimensional Euclidean spaces are [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space|Montel]] [[Hilbert space]]s but once one enters infinite-dimensional space then these two classes separate. Nuclear spaces in particular have many of the "nice" properties of finite-dimensional TVSs (e.g. the [[Schwartz kernel theorem]]) that infinite-dimensional Banach spaces lack (for more details, see the properties, sufficient conditions, and characterizations given in the article [[Nuclear space]]). It is in this sense that nuclear spaces are an "alternative generalization" of finite-dimensional spaces. Also, as a general rule, in practice most "naturally occurring" TVSs are usually either Banach spaces or nuclear space. Typically, most TVSs that are associated with smoothness (i.e. {{em|infinite}} differentiability, such as <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> and <math>C^\infty(U)</math>) end up being nuclear TVSs while TVSs associated with {{em|finite}} continuous differentiability (such as <math>C^k(K)</math> with {{mvar|K}} compact and <math>k \neq \infty</math>) often end up being non-nuclear spaces, such as Banach spaces.</ref>

===== Relationships between spaces =====

Using the [[Direct limit|universal property of direct limit]]s and the fact that the natural inclusions <math>\operatorname{In}_K^L : C^k(K) \to C^k(L)</math> are all [[topological embedding]], one may show that all of the maps <math>\operatorname{In}_K^U : C^k(K) \to C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> are also topological embeddings. Said differently, the topology on <math>C^k(K)</math> is identical to the [[subspace topology]] that it inherits from {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}, where recall that {{tmath| C^k(K) }}'s topology was {{em|defined}} to be the subspace topology induced on it by {{tmath| C^k(U) }}. In particular, both <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> and <math>C^k(U)</math> induces the same subspace topology on {{tmath| C^k(K) }}. However, this does '''{{em|not}}''' imply that the canonical LF topology on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is equal to the subspace topology induced on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> by {{tmath| C^k(U) }}; these two topologies on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> are in fact '''{{em|never}}''' equal to each other since the canonical LF topology is {{em|never}} metrizable while the subspace topology induced on it by <math>C^k(U)</math> is metrizable (since recall that <math>C^k(U)</math> is metrizable). The canonical LF topology on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is actually {{em|strictly [[Comparison of topologies|finer]]}} than the subspace topology that it inherits from <math>C^k(U)</math> (thus the natural inclusion <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)\to C^k(U)</math> is continuous but {{em|not}} a [[topological embedding]]).{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-134}}

Indeed, the canonical LF topology is so [[Comparison of topologies|fine]] that if <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to X</math> denotes some linear map that is a "natural inclusion" (such as {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to C^k(U) }}, or {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\to L^p(U) }}, or other maps discussed below) then this map will typically be continuous, which (as is explained below) is ultimately the reason why locally integrable functions, [[Radon measure]]s, etc. all induce distributions (via the transpose of such a "natural inclusion"). Said differently, the reason why there are so many different ways of defining distributions from other spaces ultimately stems from how very fine the canonical LF topology is. Moreover, since distributions are just continuous linear functionals on {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, the fine nature of the canonical LF topology means that more linear functionals on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> end up being continuous ("more" means as compared to a coarser topology that we could have placed on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> such as for instance, the subspace topology induced by some {{tmath| C^k(U) }}, which although it would have made <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> metrizable, it would have also resulted in fewer linear functionals on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> being continuous and thus there would have been fewer distributions; moreover, this particular coarser topology also has the disadvantage of not making <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> into a [[Complete topological vector space|complete TVS]]{{sfn|Rudin|1991|pp=149-155}}).

===== Other properties =====

* The differentiation map <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is a continuous linear operator.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=446-447}}
* The [[Bilinear map|bilinear multiplication map]] <math>C^\infty(\R^m) \times C_\text{c}^\infty(\R^n) \to C_\text{c}^\infty(\R^{m+n})</math> given by <math>(f,g)\mapsto fg</math> is {{em|not}} continuous; it is however, [[Hypocontinuous bilinear map|hypocontinuous]].{{sfn|Trèves|2006|p=423}}

=== Distributions ===

{{see also|Continuous linear functional}}

As discussed earlier, continuous [[Linear form|linear functionals]] on a <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> are known as distributions on {{mvar|U}}. Thus the set of all distributions on {{mvar|U}} is the [[continuous dual space]] of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, which when endowed with the [[Strong topology (polar topology)|strong dual topology]] is denoted by {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}.

{{block indent|em=1.5|text=By definition, a {{em|'''distribution''' on {{mvar|U}}}} is defined to be a [[Continuous linear operator|continuous]] [[Linear form|linear functional]] on {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}. Said differently, a distribution on {{mvar|U}} is an element of the [[continuous dual space]] of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> when <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is endowed with its canonical LF topology.}}

We have the canonical [[dual system|duality pairing]] between a distribution {{mvar|T}} on {{mvar|U}} and a test function {{tmath| f \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, which is denoted using [[angle brackets]] by
<math display=block>\begin{cases} \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) \times C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to \R \\ (T, f) \mapsto \langle T, f \rangle := T(f) \end{cases}</math>

One interprets this notation as the distribution {{mvar|T}} acting on the test function <math>f</math> to give a scalar, or symmetrically as the test function <math>f</math> acting on the distribution {{mvar|T}}.

==== Characterizations of distributions ====

'''Proposition.''' If {{mvar|T}} is a [[Linear form|linear functional]] on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> then the following are equivalent:
# {{mvar|T}} is a distribution;
# {{em|'''Definition'''}} : {{mvar|T}} is a [[continuous function]].
# {{mvar|T}} is [[Continuity at a point|continuous]] at the origin.
# {{mvar|T}} is [[Uniform continuity|uniformly continuous]].
# {{mvar|T}} is a [[bounded operator]].
# {{mvar|T}} is [[sequentially continuous]].
#* explicitly, for every sequence <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> that converges in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> to some <math>f \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U),</math> <math>\lim_{i \to \infty} T\left(f_i\right) = T(f);</math><ref group=note>Even though the topology of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is not metrizable, a linear functional on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is continuous if and only if it is sequentially continuous.</ref>
# {{mvar|T}} is [[sequentially continuous]] at the origin; in other words, {{mvar|T}} maps null sequences<ref group=note name="Def null sequence"/> to null sequences.
#* explicitly, for every sequence <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> that converges in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> to the origin (such a sequence is called a {{em|null sequence}}), <math>\lim_{i \to \infty} T\left(f_i\right) = 0.</math>
#* a {{em|null sequence}} is by definition a sequence that converges to the origin.
# {{mvar|T}} maps null sequences to bounded subsets.
#* explicitly, for every sequence <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> that converges in <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> to the origin, the sequence <math>\left(T\left(f_i\right)\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is bounded.
# {{mvar|T}} maps [[Mackey convergence|Mackey convergent]] null sequences<ref group=note name="Def of Mackey convergent"/> to bounded subsets; 
#* explicitly, for every Mackey convergent null sequence <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, the sequence <math>\left(T\left(f_i\right)\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is bounded.
#* a sequence <math>f_{\bull} = \left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is said to be {{em|[[Mackey convergence|Mackey convergent]] to {{math|0}}}} if there exists a divergent sequence <math>r_{\bull} = \left(r_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty \to \infty</math> of positive real number such that the sequence <math>\left(r_i f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is bounded; every sequence that is Mackey convergent to {{math|0}} necessarily converges to the origin (in the usual sense).
# The kernel of {{mvar|T}} is a closed subspace of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}.
# The graph of {{mvar|T}} is closed.
<!------ START: Removed information ----
* Note in particular that the following seminorms on <math>C^\infty(U)</math> (which recall were defined earlier) all restrict to continuous seminorms on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math>: {{space|1}} <math>q_{i, K},</math> {{space|1}} <math>r_{i, K},</math> {{space|1}} <math>r_{t, K},</math> and <math>s_{p, K},</math> where {{mvar|K}} is any compact subset of {{mvar|U}}, <math>i \geq 0</math> is an integer, and <math>p</math> is a multi-index. So to show that {{mvar|T}} is continuous, it {{em|suffices}} to show that the restriction to <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> of one of these seminorms, call it {{mvar|g}}, satisfies <math>| T|\leq C g</math> for some <math>C > 0.</math>
---- END: Removed information ---->
# There exists a continuous seminorm <math>g</math> on <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> such that <math>|T| \leq g.</math>
# There exists a constant <math>C > 0,</math> a collection of continuous seminorms, <math>\mathcal{P},</math> that defines the canonical LF topology of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U),</math> and a finite subset <math>\left\{g_1, \ldots, g_m\right\} \subseteq \mathcal{P}</math> such that <math>|T| \leq C(g_1 + \cdots g_m);</math><ref group=note>If <math>\mathcal{P}</math> is also a [[directed set]] under the usual function comparison then we can take the finite collection to consist of a single element.</ref>
# For every compact subset <math>K \subseteq U</math> there exist constants <math>C > 0</math> and <math>N \in \N</math> such that for all <math>f \in C^\infty(K),</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=222-223}} <math display=block>|T(f)| \leq C \sup \{|\partial^p f(x)| : x \in U, |\alpha|\leq N\}.</math>
# For every compact subset <math>K\subseteq U</math> there exist constants <math>C_K>0</math> and <math>N_K\in \N</math> such that for all <math>f \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> with [[#support of a function|support]] contained in <math>K,</math><ref name="Grubb 2009 page=14"/> <math display=block>|T(f)| \leq C_K \sup \{\left|\partial^\alpha f(x)\right| : x \in K, |\alpha|\leq N_K\}.</math>
# For any compact subset <math>K\subseteq U</math> and any sequence <math>\{f_i\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C^\infty(K),</math> if <math>\{\partial^p f_i\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> converges uniformly to zero for all [[multi-index|multi-indices]] <math>p,</math> then <math>T(f_i) \to 0.</math>
# Any of the {{em|three}} statements immediately above (that is, statements 14, 15, and 16) but with the additional requirement that compact set <math>K</math> belongs to <math>\mathbb{K}.</math>

==== Topology on the space of distributions ====

{{see also|Strong dual space|Polar topology|Dual topology|Dual system}}

{{block indent|em=1.5|text='''Definition and notation''': {{em|The '''space of distributions''' on {{mvar|U}}}}, denoted by {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}, is the [[continuous dual space]] of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> endowed with the [[Strong topology (polar topology)|topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets]] of <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U).</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-134}} More succinctly, the space of distributions on {{mvar|U}} is {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) := \left(C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\right)^{\prime}_b }}.}}

The topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets is also called {{em|the '''[[Strong dual space|strong dual topology]]'''}}.<ref group=note>In [[functional analysis]], the strong dual topology is often the "standard" or "default" topology placed on the continuous dual space <math>X',</math> where if {{mvar|X}} is a [[normed space]] then this strong dual topology is the same as the usual norm-induced topology on {{tmath| X' }}.</ref> This topology is chosen because it is with this topology that <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> becomes a [[nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space]] and it is with this topology that the [[Schwartz kernel theorem]] holds.<ref>See for example {{harvnb|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|p=173}}.</ref> No matter what dual topology is placed on <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U),</math><ref group=note>Technically, the topology must be coarser than the strong dual topology and also simultaneously be finer than the [[weak* topology]].</ref> a {{em|sequence}} of distributions converges in this topology if and only if it converges pointwise (although this need not be true of a [[Net (mathematics)|net]]). No matter which topology is chosen, <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> will be a non-[[Metrizable topological vector space|metrizable]], [[locally convex]] [[topological vector space]]. The space <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> is [[Separable space|separable]]<ref name="Gabriyelyan 2017"/> and has the [[strong Pytkeev property]]<ref name="Gabriyelyan Kakol and·Leiderman">Gabriyelyan, S.S. Kakol J., and·Leiderman, A. [https://prometeo2013058.blogs.upv.es/files/2014/02/sPp-MM.pdf "The strong Pitkeev property for topological groups and topological vector spaces"]</ref> but it is neither a [[Compactly generated space|k-space]]<ref name="Gabriyelyan Kakol and·Leiderman"/> nor a [[sequential space]],<ref name="Gabriyelyan 2017"/> which in particular implies that it is not [[Metrizable topological vector space|metrizable]] and also that its topology can {{em|not}} be defined using only sequences.

===Topological properties===

====Topological vector space categories====

<!----NOTE: Do NOT remove any of the stated properties without a GOOD reason. While some of the properties of the spaces described in this subsection are easy to show, many of them were proven long after distributions were defined because they are NON-TRIVIAL results (e.g. that some of these spaces are distinguished, barrelled, or bornological was proved by Alexander Grothendieck). So while some of these lists of properties are relatively long, properties should not be removed for the sole reason of make a list a little shorter. ----->
The canonical LF topology makes <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> into a [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] [[Distinguished space|distinguished]] [[LF-space|strict LF-space]] (and a [[LB-space|strict LB-space]] if and only if <math>k \neq \infty</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=195-201}}), which implies that <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is a [[Meager set|meager]] subset of itself.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=435}} Furthermore, {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}, as well as its [[strong dual space]], is a complete [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[locally convex]] [[Barrelled space|barrelled]] [[Bornological space|bornological]] [[Mackey space]]. The [[Strong dual space|strong dual]] of <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> is a [[Fréchet space]] if and only if <math>k \neq \infty</math> so in particular, the strong dual of {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, which is the space <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> of distributions on {{mvar|U}}, is {{em|not}} metrizable (note that the [[weak-* topology]] on <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> also is not metrizable and moreover, it further lacks almost all of the nice properties that the [[Strong topology (polar topology)|strong dual topology]] gives {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}).

The three spaces {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}, {{tmath| C^\infty(U) }}, and the [[Schwartz space]] {{tmath| \mathcal{S}(\R^n) }}, as well as the strong duals of each of these three spaces, are [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] [[Nuclear space|nuclear]]{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=526-534}} [[Montel space|Montel]]{{sfn|Trèves|2006|p=357}} [[bornological space]]s, which implies that all six of these locally convex spaces are also [[Paracompact space|paracompact]]<ref name="Encyc. Math TVS">{{cite web |title=Topological vector space |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=Encyclopedia of Mathematics |access-date=September 6, 2020 |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Topological_vector_space |quote="It is a Montel space, hence paracompact, and so normal."}}</ref> [[Reflexive space|reflexive]] [[Barrelled space|barrelled]] [[Mackey space]]s. The spaces <math>C^\infty(U)</math> and <math>\mathcal{S}(\R^n)</math> are both [[Distinguished space|distinguished]] [[Fréchet space]]s. Moreover, both <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> and <math>\mathcal{S}(\R^n)</math> are [[Schwartz topological vector space|Schwartz TVSs]].

==== Convergent sequences ====

===== Convergent sequences and their insufficiency to describe topologies =====

The strong dual spaces of <math>C^\infty(U)</math> and <math>\mathcal{S}(\R^n)</math> are [[sequential space]]s but not [[Fréchet-Urysohn space]]s.<ref name="Gabriyelyan 2017"/> Moreover, neither the space of test functions <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> nor its strong dual <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> is a [[sequential space]] (not even an [[Ascoli space]]),<ref name="Gabriyelyan 2017">Gabriyelyan, Saak [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1702.07867.pdf "Topological properties of Strict LF-spaces and strong duals of Montel Strict LF-spaces"] (2017)</ref><ref name="Shirai 1959">T. Shirai, Sur les Topologies des Espaces de L. Schwartz, Proc. Japan Acad. 35 (1959), 31-36.</ref> which in particular implies that their topologies can {{em|not}} be defined entirely in terms of convergent sequences.

A sequence <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> converges in <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> if and only if there exists some <math>K \in \mathbb{K}</math> such that <math>C^k(K)</math> contains this sequence and this sequence converges in <math>C^k(K)</math>; equivalently, it converges if and only if the following two conditions hold:<ref>According to {{harvnb|Gel'fand|Shilov|1966–1968|loc=v. 1, §1.2}}</ref>
# There is a compact set <math>K \subseteq U</math> containing the supports of all <math>f_i.</math>
# For each [[multi-index]] <math>\alpha,</math> the sequence of partial derivatives <math>\partial^\alpha f_{i}</math> tends [[uniform convergence|uniformly]] to <math>\partial^\alpha f.</math>

Neither the space <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> nor its strong dual <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> is a [[sequential space]],<ref name="Gabriyelyan 2017"/><ref name="Shirai 1959"/> and consequently, their topologies can '''{{em|not}}''' be defined entirely in terms of convergent sequences. For this reason, the above characterization of when a sequence converges is {{em|not}} enough to define the canonical LF topology on {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }}. The same can be said of the strong dual topology on {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}.

===== What sequences do characterize =====

Nevertheless, sequences do characterize many important properties, as we now discuss. It is known that in the [[Continuous dual space|dual space]] of any Montel space, a sequence converges in the [[Strong dual space|strong dual topology]] if and only if it converges in the [[weak* topology]],{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=351-359}} which in particular, is the reason why a sequence of distributions converges (in the strong dual topology) if and only if it converges pointwise (this leads many authors to use [[pointwise convergence]] to actually {{em|define}} the convergence of a sequence of distributions; this is fine for sequences but it does {{em|not}} extend to the convergence of [[Net (mathematics)|nets]] of distributions since a net may converge pointwise but fail to converge in the strong dual topology).

Sequences characterize continuity of linear maps valued in locally convex space. Suppose {{mvar|X}} is a locally convex [[bornological space]] (such as any of the six TVSs mentioned earlier). Then a linear map <math>F : X \to Y</math> into a locally convex space {{mvar|Y}} is continuous if and only if it maps null sequences<ref group=note name="Def null sequence">A '''{{em|null sequence}}''' is a sequence that converges to the origin.</ref> in {{mvar|X}} to [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded subsets]] of {{mvar|Y}}.<ref group=note>Recall that a linear map is bounded if and only if it maps null sequences to bounded sequences.</ref> More generally, such a linear map <math>F : X \to Y</math> is continuous if and only if it maps [[Mackey convergence|Mackey convergent]] null sequences<ref group=note name="Def of Mackey convergent">A sequence <math>x_{\bull} = \left(x_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is said to be {{em|Mackey convergent to {{math|0}} in <math>X,</math>}} if there exists a divergent sequence <math>r_{\bull} = \left(r_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty \to \infty</math> of positive real number such that <math>\left(r_i x_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a bounded set in <math>X.</math></ref> to bounded subsets of <math>Y.</math> So in particular, if a linear map <math>F : X \to Y</math> into a locally convex space is [[sequentially continuous]] at the origin then it is continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441-457}} However, this does {{em|not}} necessarily extend to non-linear maps and/or to maps valued in topological spaces that are not locally convex TVSs.

For every <math>k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, \infty\}, C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is [[sequentially dense]] in {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=150-160}} Furthermore, <math>\{D_\phi : \phi \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\}</math> is a sequentially dense subset of <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> (with its strong dual topology){{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=300-304}} and also a sequentially dense subset of the strong dual space of <math>C^\infty(U).</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=300-304}}

===== Sequences of distributions =====
{{main|Limit of distributions}}

A sequence of distributions <math>(T_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> converges with respect to the weak-* topology on <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> to a distribution {{mvar|T}} if and only if
<math display=block>\langle T_i, f \rangle \to \langle T, f \rangle</math>
for every test function <math>f \in \mathcal{D}(U).</math> For example, if <math>f_m:\R\to\R</math> is the function
<math display=block>f_m(x) = \begin{cases} m & \text{ if } x \in [0,\frac{1}{m}] \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise } \end{cases}</math>
and <math>T_m</math> is the distribution corresponding to <math>f_m,</math> then
<math display=block>\langle T_m, f \rangle = m \int_0^{\frac{1}{m}} f(x)\, dx \to f(0) = \langle \delta, f \rangle</math>
as <math>m \to \infty,</math> so <math>T_m \to \delta</math> in <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\R).</math> Thus, for large <math>m,</math> the function <math>f_m</math> can be regarded as an approximation of the Dirac delta distribution.

===== Other properties =====

* The strong dual space of <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> is TVS isomorphic to <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> via the canonical TVS-isomorphism <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to (\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U))'_{b}</math> defined by sending <math>f \in C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> to {{em|value at <math>f</math>}} (that is, to the linear functional on <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> defined by sending <math>d \in \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> to {{tmath| d(f) }});
* On any bounded subset of <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U),</math> the weak and strong subspace topologies coincide; the same is true for {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty(U) }};
* Every weakly convergent sequence in <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> is strongly convergent (although this does not extend to [[Net (mathematics)|nets]]).

== Localization of distributions ==

=== Preliminaries: Transpose of a linear operator ===
{{anchor|Transpose of a linear operator}}
{{main|Transpose of a linear map}}

Operations on distributions and spaces of distributions are often defined by means of the [[Transpose of a linear map|transpose]] of a linear operator. This is because the transpose allows for a unified presentation of the many definitions in the theory of distributions and also because its properties are well known in [[functional analysis]].<ref>{{harvnb|Strichartz|1994|loc=§2.3}}; {{harvnb|Trèves|2006}}.</ref> For instance, the well-known [[Hermitian adjoint]] of a linear operator between [[Hilbert space]]s is just the operator's transpose (but with the [[Riesz representation theorem]] used to identify each Hilbert space with its [[Strong dual space|continuous dual space]]). In general the transpose of a continuous linear map <math>A : X \to Y</math> is the linear map 
<math display=block>{}^\text{t}\!A : Y' \to X' \qquad \text{ defined by } \qquad {}^\text{t}\! A(y') := y' \circ A,</math> 
or equivalently, it is the unique map satisfying <math>\langle y', A(x)\rangle = \left\langle {}^\text{t}\! A (y'), x \right\rangle</math> for all <math>x \in X</math> and all <math>y' \in Y'</math> (the prime symbol in <math>y'</math> does not denote a derivative of any kind; it merely indicates that <math>y'</math> is an element of the continuous dual space <math>Y'</math>). Since <math>A</math> is continuous, the transpose <math>{}^\text{t}\! A : Y' \to X'</math> is also continuous when both duals are endowed with their respective [[Strong dual space|strong dual topologies]]; it is also continuous when both duals are endowed with their respective [[Weak* topology|weak* topologies]] (see the articles [[Polar topology#Polar topologies and topological vector spaces|polar topology]] and [[Dual system#Weak topology|dual system]] for more details).

In the context of distributions, the characterization of the transpose can be refined slightly. Let <math>A : \mathcal{D}(U) \to \mathcal{D}(U)</math> be a continuous linear map. Then by definition, the transpose of <math>A</math> is the unique linear operator <math>A^t : \mathcal{D}'(U) \to \mathcal{D}'(U)</math> that satisfies:
<math display=block>\langle {}^\text{t}\! A(T), \phi \rangle = \langle T, A(\phi) \rangle \quad \text{ for all } \phi \in \mathcal{D}(U) \text{ and all } T \in \mathcal{D}'(U).</math>

Since <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> is dense in <math>\mathcal{D}'(U)</math> (here, <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> actually refers to the set of distributions <math>\left\{D_\psi : \psi \in \mathcal{D}(U)\right\}</math>) it is sufficient that the defining equality hold for all distributions of the form <math>T = D_\psi</math> where <math>\psi \in \mathcal{D}(U).</math> Explicitly, this means that a continuous linear map <math>B : \mathcal{D}'(U) \to \mathcal{D}'(U)</math> is equal to <math>{}^\text{t}\! A</math> if and only if the condition below holds:
<math display=block>\langle B(D_\psi), \phi \rangle = \langle {}^\text{t}\! A(D_\psi), \phi \rangle \quad \text{ for all } \phi, \psi \in \mathcal{D}(U)</math>
where the right hand side equals <math>\langle {}^\text{t}\! A(D_\psi), \phi \rangle = \langle D_\psi, A(\phi) \rangle = \langle \psi, A(\phi) \rangle = \int_U \psi \cdot A(\phi) \,dx.</math>

=== Extensions and restrictions to an open subset ===

Let <math>V \subseteq U</math> be open subsets of {{tmath| \R^n }}. 
Every function <math>f \in \mathcal{D}(V)</math> can be {{em|extended by zero}} from its domain <math>V</math> to a function on <math>U</math> by setting it equal to <math>0</math> on the [[Complement (set theory)|complement]] <math>U \setminus V.</math> This extension is a smooth compactly supported function called the {{em|trivial extension of <math>f</math> to <math>U</math>}} and it will be denoted by {{tmath| E_{VU} (f) }}.
This assignment <math>f \mapsto E_{VU} (f)</math> defines the {{em|trivial extension}} operator 
<math>E_{VU} : \mathcal{D}(V) \to \mathcal{D}(U),</math> 
which is a continuous injective linear map. It is used to canonically identify <math>\mathcal{D}(V)</math> as a [[vector subspace]] of <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> (although {{em|not}} as a [[topological subspace]]). 
Its transpose ([[#Transpose of a linear operator|explained here]]) 
<math display=block>\rho_{VU} := {}^\text{t}\! E_{VU} : \mathcal{D}'(U) \to \mathcal{D}'(V),</math> 
is called the '''{{em|{{visible anchor|restriction map|text=restriction to <math>V</math> of distributions in <math>U</math>}}}}'''{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}} and as the name suggests, the image <math>\rho_{VU}(T)</math> of a distribution <math>T \in \mathcal{D}'(U)</math> under this map is a distribution on <math>V</math> called the '''restriction of <math>T</math> to <math>V.</math>''' The [[#Transpose of a linear operator|defining condition]] of the restriction <math>\rho_{VU}(T)</math> is:
<math display=block>\langle \rho_{VU} T, \phi \rangle = \langle T, E_{VU} \phi \rangle \quad \text{ for all } \phi \in \mathcal{D}(V).</math>
If <math>V \neq U</math> then the (continuous injective linear) trivial extension map <math>E_{VU} : \mathcal{D}(V) \to \mathcal{D}(U)</math> is {{em|not}} a topological embedding (in other words, if this linear injection was used to identify <math>\mathcal{D}(V)</math> as a subset of <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> then <math>\mathcal{D}(V)</math>'s topology would [[Comparison of topologies|strictly finer]] than the [[subspace topology]] that <math>\mathcal{D}(U)</math> induces on it; importantly, it would {{em|not}} be a [[topological subspace]] since that requires equality of topologies) and its range is also {{em|not}} dense in its codomain <math>\mathcal{D}(U).</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}} Consequently, if <math>V \neq U</math> then [[#restriction map|the restriction mapping]] is neither injective nor surjective.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}} A distribution <math>S \in \mathcal{D}'(V)</math> is said to be '''{{em|extendible to {{mvar|U}}}}''' if it belongs to the range of the transpose of <math>E_{VU}</math> and it is called '''{{em|extendible}}''' if it is extendable to <math>\R^n.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=245-247}}

Unless {{tmath|1= U = V }}, the restriction to <math>V</math> is neither [[injective]] nor [[surjective]].

== Spaces of distributions ==

For all <math>0 < k < \infty</math> and all {{tmath| 1 < p < \infty }}, all of the following canonical injections are continuous and have an [[Image of a function|image/range]] that is a [[Dense set|dense subset]] of their codomain:{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-135}}{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=240-245}}
<math display=block>\begin{matrix}
C_\text{c}^\infty(U) & \to & C_\text{c}^k(U) & \to & C_\text{c}^0(U) & \to & L_\text{c}^\infty(U) & \to & L_\text{c}^{p+1}(U) & \to & L_\text{c}^p(U) & \to & L_\text{c}^1(U) \\
\downarrow & &\downarrow && \downarrow && && &&  && && \\
C^\infty(U) & \to & C^k(U) & \to & C^0(U)  && && &&  && &&
\end{matrix}</math>
where the topologies on the [[LB-space]]s <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> are the canonical LF topologies as [[#compactly supported Lp space|defined below]] (so in particular, they are not the usual norm topologies). 
The range of each of the maps above (and of any composition of the maps above) is dense in the codomain. Indeed, <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U)</math> is even [[sequentially dense]] in every {{tmath| C_\text{c}^k(U) }}.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=150-160}} For every <math>1 \leq p \leq \infty,</math> the canonical inclusion <math>C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to L^p(U)</math> into the normed space <math>L^p(U)</math> (here <math>L^p(U)</math> has its [[Lp space|usual norm topology]]) is a continuous linear injection and the range of this injection is dense in its codomain if and only if {{tmath| p \neq \infty }}.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=240-245}}

Suppose that <math>X</math> is one of the LF-spaces <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> (for <math>k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, \infty\}</math>) or LB-spaces <math>L^p_\text{c}(U)</math> (for <math>1 \leq p \leq \infty</math>) or normed spaces [[Lp space|<math>L^p(U)</math>]] (for {{tmath| 1 \leq p < \infty }}).{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=240-245}} Because the canonical injection <math>\operatorname{In}_X : C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to X</math> is a continuous injection whose image is dense in the codomain, this map's [[Transpose of a linear map|transpose]] <math>{}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In}_X : X'_b \to \mathcal{D}'(U) = \left(C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\right)'_b</math> is a continuous injection. This injective transpose map thus allows the [[continuous dual space]] <math>X'</math> of <math>X</math> to be identified with a certain vector subspace of the space <math>\mathcal{D}'(U)</math> of all distributions (specifically, it is identified with the image of this transpose map). This continuous transpose map is not necessarily a TVS-embedding so the topology that this map transfers from its domain to the image <math>\operatorname{Im}\left({}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In}_X\right)</math> is finer than the subspace topology that this space inherits from {{tmath| \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}. 
A linear subspace of <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)</math> carrying a locally convex topology that is finer than the subspace topology induced by <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) = \left(C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\right)^{\prime}_b</math> is called '''{{em|a space of distributions}}'''.{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=240-252}} 
Almost all of the spaces of distributions mentioned in this article arise in this way (e.g. tempered distribution, restrictions, distributions of order <math>\leq</math> some integer, distributions induced by a positive Radon measure, distributions induced by an <math>L^p</math>-function, etc.) and any representation theorem about the dual space of {{mvar|X}} may, through the transpose {{tmath| {}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In}_X : X'_b \to \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) }}, be transferred directly to elements of the space {{tmath| \operatorname{Im} \left({}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In}_X\right) }}.

=== Compactly supported ''L<sup>p</sup>''-spaces ===

Given {{tmath| 1 \leq p \leq \infty }}, the vector space <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> of {{visible anchor|compactly supported Lp space|text=compactly supported [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math> functions]]}} on <math>U</math> and its topology are defined as direct limits of the spaces <math>L_\text{c}^p(K)</math> in a manner analogous to how the canonical LF-topologies on <math>C_\text{c}^k(U)</math> were defined. 
For any compact {{tmath| K \subseteq U }}, let <math>L^p(K)</math> denote the set of all element in <math>L^p(U)</math> (which recall are [[equivalence class]] of Lebesgue measurable <math>L^p</math> functions on <math>U</math>) having a representative <math>f</math> whose support (which recall is the closure of <math>\{u \in U : f(x) \neq 0\}</math> in <math>U</math>) is a subset of <math>K</math> (such an <math>f</math> is almost everywhere defined in {{tmath| K }}). 
The set <math>L^p(K)</math> is a closed vector subspace <math>L^p(U)</math> and is thus a [[Banach space]] and when <math>p = 2,</math> even a [[Hilbert space]].{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-135}} 
Let <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> be the union of all <math>L^p(K)</math> as <math>K \subseteq U</math> ranges over all compact subsets of <math>U.</math> 
The set <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> is a vector subspace of <math>L^p(U)</math> whose elements are the (equivalence classes of) compactly supported <math>L^p</math> functions defined on <math>U</math> (or almost everywhere on {{tmath| U }}). 
Endow <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> with the [[final topology]] (direct limit topology) induced by the inclusion maps <math>L^p(K) \to L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> as <math>K \subseteq U</math> ranges over all compact subsets of {{tmath| U }}. 
This topology is called the {{em|canonical LF topology}} and it is equal to the final topology induced by any [[countable set]] of inclusion maps <math>L^p(K_n) \to L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> (<math>n = 1, 2, \ldots</math>) where <math>K_1 \subseteq K_2 \subseteq \cdots</math> are any compact sets with union equal to <math>U.</math>{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=131-135}} 
This topology makes <math>L_\text{c}^p(U)</math> into an [[LB-space]] (and thus also an [[LF-space]]) with a topology that is strictly finer than the norm (subspace) topology that <math>L^p(U)</math> induces on it.

=== Radon measures ===

The inclusion map <math>\operatorname{In} : C_\text{c}^\infty(U) \to C_\text{c}^0(U)</math> is a continuous injection whose image is dense in its codomain, so the [[transpose]] <math>{}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In} : \left(C_\text{c}^0(U)\right)^{\prime}_b \to \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) = \left(C_\text{c}^\infty(U)\right)^{\prime}_b</math> is also a continuous injection.

Note that the continuous dual space <math>\left(C_\text{c}^0(U)\right)^{\prime}_b</math> can be identified as the space of [[Radon measure]]s, where there is a one-to-one correspondence between the continuous linear functionals <math>T \in \left(C_\text{c}^0(U)\right)^{\prime}_b</math> and integral with respect to a Radon measure; that is,
* if <math>T \in \left(C_\text{c}^0(U)\right)^{\prime}_b</math> then there exists a Radon measure <math>\mu</math> on {{mvar|U}} such that for all <math>f \in C_\text{c}^0(U), T(f) = \textstyle \int_U f \, d\mu,</math> and
* if <math>\mu</math> is a Radon measure on {{mvar|U}} then the linear functional on <math>C_\text{c}^0(U)</math> defined by <math>C_\text{c}^0(U) \ni f \mapsto \textstyle \int_U f \, d\mu</math> is continuous.

Through the injection <math>{}^\text{t}\! \operatorname{In} : \left(C_\text{c}^0(U)\right)^{\prime}_b \to \mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U),</math> every Radon measure becomes a distribution on {{mvar|U}}. If <math>f</math> is a [[locally integrable]] function on {{mvar|U}} then the distribution <math>\phi \mapsto \textstyle \int_U f(x) \phi(x) \, dx</math> is a Radon measure; so Radon measures form a large and important space of distributions.

The following is the theorem of the structure of distributions of [[Radon measure]]s, which shows that every Radon measure can be written as a sum of derivatives of locally <math>L^\infty</math> functions in {{mvar|U}}:

{{math theorem|name='''Theorem.'''{{sfn|Trèves|2006|pp=262–264}}|math_statement=
Suppose <math>T \in \mathcal{D}'(U)</math> is a Radon measure, where <math>U \subseteq \R^n,</math> let <math>V \subseteq U</math> be a neighborhood of the support of <math>T,</math> and let <math>I = \{p \in \N^n : |p| \leq n\}.</math> There exists a family <math>f=(f_p)_{p\in I}</math> of locally <math>L^\infty</math> functions on {{mvar|U}} such that <math>\operatorname{supp} f_p \subseteq V</math> for every {{tmath| p\in I }}, and
<math display=block>T = \sum_{p\in I} \partial^p f_p.</math>
Furthermore, <math>T</math> is also equal to a finite sum of derivatives of continuous functions on <math>U,</math> where each derivative has order <math>\leq 2 n.</math>
}}

'''Positive Radon measures'''

A linear function {{mvar|T}} on a space of functions is called '''{{em|positive}}''' if whenever a function <math>f</math> that belongs to the domain of {{mvar|T}} is non-negative (meaning that <math>f</math> is real-valued and {{tmath| f \geq 0 }}) then {{tmath| T(f) \geq 0 }}. One may show that every [[positive linear functional]] on <math>C_\text{c}^0(U)</math> is necessarily continuous (that is, necessarily a Radon measure).{{sfn|Trèves|2006|p=218}} 
[[Lebesgue measure]] is an example of a positive Radon measure.

==== Locally integrable functions as distributions ====

One particularly important class of Radon measures are those that are induced locally integrable functions. The function <math>f : U \to \R</math> is called '''{{em|locally integrable}}''' if it is [[Lebesgue integration|Lebesgue integrable]] over every compact subset {{mvar|K}} of {{mvar|U}}.<ref group=note>For more information on such class of functions, see the [[Locally integrable|entry on locally integrable functions]].</ref> This is a large class of functions which includes all continuous functions and all [[Lp space]] <math>L^p</math> functions.
